# Hard-to-vary report: “KIC 8462852 – Where’s the flux?”

## 1. The question, frozen
The title and abstract fix one question: **what produces the aperiodic dips, up to ~20%, in KIC 8462852’s flux?** This is a “what produces it?” question (forward, from causes). The paper answers neighbouring questions too — what the star is, what it is not — but those are characterisation. The explanatory claim is the occultation scenario. Range: the four-year Kepler light curve, with follow-up data 2014–2015. I freeze on the production question.

## 2. The explanation in parts
The favoured claim (§5.4, §6): a family of exocomet/planetesimal fragments, all from one earlier break-up, sharing a single highly eccentric (comet-like) orbit, whose dust clumps occult the star near pericenter.

Parts, in the owner’s words:
- **P1** the occulting material is dust
- **P2** the dust sits in discrete, star-sized clumps
- **P3** clumps at pericenter ≈0.1–1 AU, distance decoupled from orbital period
- **P4** the orbit is highly eccentric (e≈1)
- **P5** the fragments share one orbit
- **P6** one earlier break-up (tidal or thermal)
- **P7** a progenitor rocky body ≈100 km, ≈3×10²¹ g
- **P8** grains large enough to make a “forward tail”
- **P9** the star is an ordinary F3V main-sequence star
- **P10** the 0.88 d signal is rotation, not pulsation
- **P11** no IR excess because at WISE time the clumps were far from the star

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P1 dust | **Held** | The depth, duration and gradient constraints only close for an opaque dust clump about stellar size; a solid body is too large or too slow |
| P2 clumps | **Held** | By the clustered, superimposed, varying-shape dips (§2.1, §4) |
| P3 pericenter 0.1–1 AU | **Held** | Forced by the pull in §5.4 (below) |
| P4 eccentric orbit | **Held** | The linchpin: remove it and the steep gradient fights the non-repetition |
| P5 shared orbit | **Held if** | Needed so that “we have observed all the clumps”; rests on P6 being real |
| P6 one break-up | **Loose** | Paper says the mechanism “is not defined for this scenario” |
| P7 100 km body | **Loose** | The mass spans a factor ~100 with grain size; it is a lower limit |
| P8 forward tail | **Two routes** | Either large grains override radiation pressure, or two dips sit superimposed — either does the job; names both |
| P9 F3V star | **Held** | Measured spectrum |
| P10 rotation | **Held** | γ Dor STFTs do not drift; this one does |
| P11 no IR by timing | **Held if** | A timing rescue; needs a gauge |

The “more clumps further along the orbit” clause is a **catch-all**, allowed only because Figure 11 supplies a gauge (the WISE limit). All other working parts are **borrowed** from dust physics and comet behaviour.

## 4. Whole-explanation checks
**Flip.** The scenario’s central move, the eccentric pericenter, exists only to reconcile the steep gradient with the non-repetition. A periodic dip set would have needed no such move. So the move is held by the aperiodicity it was built to explain — not equally good against both outcomes.

**Direction.** Mostly forward, but σ_tot and the mass are read *backwards* from the light curve — legitimate for “what can we tell,” not yet “what is there.”

**Answer hidden in the starting points?** “Comet-like” partly names the orbit rather than deriving it; but the constraints do force eccentricity, so it is not circular.

**Where the jobs came from.** All the jobs are **given** by the observations; I added none.

**Pairs that pull.** P3 (close pericenter, for gradient and transit probability) pulls against P7 (mass): a closer pericenter raises the derived mass. The paper says so (§5.4), and the line is drawn at τ=0.2.

**Catch-alls and gauges.** “More clumps” and “any material not contributing to the dips” are the bin; the WISE upper limit is the gauge. Present, so allowed, but loose.

**What the change list leaves out.** The wavelength-dependence of the obscuration (never measured); a real repeat; the system’s age.

**Rivals.** The giant impact (§5.2) is the nearest. It is *separable*: it predicts a ~750-day repeat and a rising mid-IR excess; the comet scenario predicts spread-out fragments and no repeat. A real change tells them apart, so their disagreement is live, not verbal.

**Where the parts came from.** P1, P4, P9 are **built**; P6 is **asserted**; P7 is built but soft; P2–P5 are **fitted** to the one light curve — held only on the cases they met; P11 is fitted to the single WISE epoch.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary
The tightening moves: catch the next dip and measure its wavelength-dependence (tests P1 directly); measure the companion’s motion to settle bound versus unbound (tests P5–P6); take a second IR epoch (tests P11). The single strongest: a repeat of the fragments on the same orbit, with the same forward-tail asymmetry.

## 6. What this does not show
Hard to vary is not the same as true. The scenario is more constrained than its rivals; passing shows it sticks its neck out, not that it is right. P6 and P7 remain asserted or fitted.

## 7. One next step
Write down, before looking, what the next dip must look like under P8 — shape, asymmetry, wavelength behaviour — and commit to it.
